title: Theory-Scale Auto-Formalization of Logic for Computer Science
claim: A single source text is converted into a structured formal repository, from which multiple task-specific benchmark tracks are derived.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right with block arrows, stacked track boxes at right
description: The figure reads left to right in three stages joined by two large blue block arrows. On the left is a stack of textbook pages with the cover of 'Logic for Computer Science' on top, labeled 'Textbook'. In the middle is a window-style code browser titled 'LCS', with a Lean repository file tree on the left (CutElim, FirstOrder, Herbrand, and others, with Soundness.lean highlighted) and Lean source code with line numbers on the right. On the right, three stacked track boxes are labeled 'IAF Track: Item-Level Auto-Formalization', 'SSAF Track: Subsection-Level Auto-Formalization', and 'ITP Track: Item-Level Theorem Proving'. Each box has column headers such as Textbook Item, Context, Skeleton, and Answer, and the Answer column is highlighted orange. Blue outlines dominate the figure, and captions sit below each stage.
caption: An overview of LCS-Bench. Tracks of datasets are generated from the Lean repository derived from the textbook, covering a wide range of auto-formalization and theorem-proving tasks.
abstract: Auto-formalization is critical for scalable formal verification, but existing progress largely focuses on isolated statements, while theory-scale auto-formalization, which coherently translates hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems, remains open due to challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness. In this paper, we introduce LCS-Bench, a stand-alone, theory-scale benchmark based on Logic for Computer Science. LCS-Bench is built through a novel semi-automated agentic pipeline that leverages concept graphs, formal signature planning, issue tracking, sorry-filling with counter-example search, complemented by faithfulness review from human experts. The resulting artifact covers 327 textbook items, over 4,076 Lean declarations, and more than 85K lines of Lean code. The dataset supports broad evaluation through a data engine that automatically derives five tracks of evaluation benchmarks, measuring different aspects of auto-formalization and theorem-proving capabilities. We also introduce a novel evaluation protocol featuring definitional equivalence checkers, enabling more fine-grained and faithful assessment. Through extensive evaluation on 17 models, we demonstrate that (1) LCS-Bench is of high quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) the benchmark is challenging, with state-of-the-art models achieving only 20.3% on auto-formalization tasks; and (3) our analysis reveals key findings regarding theory-scale auto-formalization and suggests promising directions for future work.
